en: Let him cut the willow on the hillside;
The khan of Bukhara, Temir Khan,
Let him restrain his shameless daughter!
If this daughter will not be restrained,
Let him gather the peoples of eight khans,
Or have her married to someone.
This daughter who goes about astray,
Let him restrain her like this!
In her old age, a horse of hers
She leads, saying, 'I shall race him.'
If the horse she races lumbers along,
And falls behind, floundering,
Will they not call her that man's shameless
Widowed daughter?
The eight khans will ridicule us,
And afterward devour us, will they not?
Will they not call her his daughter
Who scattered so much wealth and gold?
Wandering on foot toward Bukhara,
Will they not call her his daughter who fled?
A woman who goes wrong never comes to good.
Those accursed creatures called females
Will surely never come to good.
Look at the unbeliever's
Wild excitement while a widow!
Saying, 'I shall race a horse in Bukhara,'
Look at her arrogance!
This woman, in men's clothes,
Look how she has dressed!
Delighted at her husband's death,
Look at her rejoicing!
Listen, people; listen, khan.
All of you, the whole people, listen.
Such is the salt of our Bukhara:
A young falcon that comes finds ease;
A wanderer that comes grows rich.
If one stays six years in Bukhara,
One's heart becomes perfectly at ease.
Not acknowledging God at all,
Such a wanderer comes and grows rich.
Let him gather the peoples of eight khans;
If Temir Khan will heed advice,
Let him restrain this wandering daughter.
Let her stop spurring on to race a horse,
And not have people call her Temir Khan's
Shameless daughter."
Saying this, the assembled people,
Bending their knees to the ground,
Before Temir Khan
Came in, speaking ill of her;
All his people came running.
Treading the ground where she walked,
They began crying out,
Speaking ill of Kanykey:
"Sire, dislike us if you will,
Cut down the willow on the knoll;
Restrain your wayward daughter!
From this city of Bukhara,
Gather those burdened by sorrow and regret;
Restrain your shameless daughter!
From Bukhara, whose food one savors,
God has cursed your salt.
Rejoicing at her husband's death,
Dressing in men's clothes,
Taking the direct road of corruption,
Leading a horse grown old,
Saying, 'I shall race him,'
God has cursed your daughter!
Your daughter has grown arrogant.
God has cursed her beyond measure!
Will they not call her Temir Khan's wandering daughter?
Will they not devour us thus?
Will she not disgrace us?
Will she not slaughter us thus?
Gather all the people;
Restrain this daughter of yours!"
After his people spoke like this,
The khan of Bukhara, Temir Khan,
Heard their narrow-mindedness.
Thus he felt deeply ashamed.
Rebuking his many people,
Temir Khan grew resolute:
"Your swan-white-bearded elders—
May God take all of you!
Slandering my own child,
You meant to burn my soul!
In this city of Bukhara
I became sovereign in my youth.
At first I had no children.
Among females, I saw a skilled one;
I had thirteen daughters in succession.
The youngest of twelve daughters,
God's beloved servant,
This Kanykey here,
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims.
When she reached six years old,
I cherished her and braided her hair.
More than sixty ranks of men,
Even today I love her.
The reason I love her:
She went to the caliph and received a letter;
She received a blessing from the prince.
When she reached twelve years old,
She was named the Tigress.
When she reached thirteen,
Samarkand, Kokand, Andijan—
She laid them waste and took six.
When she reached fourteen,
From Baghdad and Egypt
They studied with her for eight months.
Saying, 'Fierce Kanykey has risen from Bukhara,'
Those who heard her fame were afraid.
When she reached fourteen,
The khan of Kakan grieved.
Saying, 'A fierce woman who will know my worth,'
Leopard Khan Manas heard and rejoiced.
When she reached fourteen,
We dedicated and slaughtered a white-gray mare.
Khan Bakay intervened,
And we became close in-laws.
When she completed her fourteenth year,
Her household settled in Talas,
And she became Manas's wife.
My valiant child Kanykey
Did not stand idly by.
For the valiant gray-maned Manas,
She gathered what was scattered,
She joined what was severed.
Planting, she made a garden;
Building, she made a house.
Illustrious Manas
She made khan over the world's people.
Making her imposing head a banner,
She made her woman's self a hero.
Her gray-maned khan Manas
She made a lion for the many people.
Preparing arrowproof coats,
Preparing abundant ammunition,
Preparing an army like forty nobles,
She raided Ombu and took ten.
She took a thousand black-eyed ones,
And took gold coins loaded on elephants.
Gathering forty-two hosts of troops,
For forty-two hosts of people
She gathered many coats of gold.
She made her mighty Manas khan,
And made him a man of sacred virtue.
In the Beijing of Kakan Khan,
She made Manas khan for six months.
'Kanykey, the people's leader,
How could she do such a thing?
Without shame, men's clothes—
With what face could she wear them?
How could Kanykey
Lead her aged horse,
Saying, "I shall race him"?' you say."
Unable to die of shame,
Unable to take his own life,
Khan Temir's golden throne,
With a plane-tree garden in its midst—
If soaked in water forty years,
Not the slightest edge would fade;
If soaked for eighty years,
It would not loosen and rot.
Of gold-patterned carpets,
Sixty were spread out.
Of Temir Khan's tower,
Do not ask about the watch-post's splendor.
Hearing words from his wayward people,
Temir Khan was choked with emotion.
When he came out from the watch-post and looked,
His dear child Kanykey
Had tightly gathered her girth-thick hair,
And tied it upon her crown.
Her arrowproof armor,
She had put it all on together.
Her sword, axe, and spear
She had hung in their proper places.
Black-steel Zulpukor
She had fastened snugly at her wrist.
The double-edged Aktinte
She had drawn from its sheath.
She had dressed in men's clothes,
Trampling over the peoples of eight khans,
There went my child Kanykey.
Those who saw her were unsettled.
If you looked at each part of her body,
Her husband who had passed away,
Manas—how much she looked like him!
From her mouth, blue flame
Darted aside and hissed.
Her formidable teeth, like a gate,
Scattered like grains of millet.
Those who came straight before her
Split apart and scurried away,
Calling out greetings.
She had raised tremendous uproar.
"My foal, my child Kanykey,
Taytoru, sixty years of maturity,
You lead, saying, 'I shall race him.'
My foal, my child Kanykey,
God has blessed this fierce woman."
When he saw Kanykey,
Was Temir Khan not a khan?
Seeing the distress,
He was deeply grieved and ashamed.
"Since Kanykey has become like this,
Who would not become like this?" he said.
Waving his hands in anguish,
Offended with Kanykey, he said:
"Hey, Kanykey, my foal,
Turn your horse's head this way.
My honor is gone, Kanykey.
Stand here in front!
While your head is still upon your shoulders,
My foal, do not settle along the river.
Letting them call you a desperate woman—
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
Do not become the people's laughingstock!
You have no support to lean on,
My valiant child Kanykey.
To make your horse race more strongly,
To stand upon the ridge and shout,
Your renowned lion Manas is not here.
Saying, 'I shall race a horse,' Kanykey,
Do not go astray without cause.
Blustering, Kanykey,
Do not seek to count up heaps of gold.
Becoming a laughingstock to many khans,
My foal, do not race your Taytoru.
While your head is still upon your shoulders,
Do not settle along the river.
Letting them call you a desperate woman,
My dear Kanykey,
Do not become the people's laughingstock!
My child, you have no support to lean on,
No secure place of your own,
Who subdued every place he faced—
Those who opposed him,
He seized and broke them.
Your panther, lion Manas, is gone.
You have no grounds to enter a race.
To shout encouragement aloud,
Your fortunate Kyrgyz people are gone.
Living widowed, my foal,
Do not grow rash without cause.
O Kanykey, my foal,
My little one born to good fortune,
With eight hundred households in your hands,
Kanykey, have you suffered want of people?
You have all four kinds of livestock.
Kanykey, have you suffered want of wealth?
O Kanykey, my foal,
From palm-sized Bukhara,
I myself, though I am khan,
